newsitem.title: UK: Senior Conservative defects to UK Referendum Party.
newsitem.headline: Senior Conservative defects to UK Referendum Party.

text.p: Britain's embattled Conservatives were rocked on Sunday by news that a senior member of the ruling party was defecting to the new Referendum Party run by millionaire tycoon Sir James Goldsmith.
Lord McAlpine, a former treasurer and deputy chairman of the Conservatives, made the announcement on the eve of the Conservative Party's last annual conference before an imminent general election.
McAlpine will disclose his decision -- expected to widen already deep rifts among the Conservatives over Europe -- on Monday's edition of the BBC's Panorama programme at 2030 gmt.
Goldsmith's Referendum Party has shaken the Conservative Party to its foundations by planning to fight the next election with a demand for a referendum over Britain's future in the European Union.
Although McAlpine has criticised Prime Minister John Major's leadership of the Conservative Party, few thought he would actually take this drastic step.

McAlpine told the BBC he had already confided in former Conservative prime minister Margaret Thatcher, under whom he served, about his change of allegiance and that he was not afraid of being branded a traitor.
He said: "People talk in terms of traitors and they blame people for changing their minds. I mean, for God's sake, it's a mobile thing, politics.
"I don't need any converting to the point of view of the Referendum Party. I need converting back to the Conservative Party because they don't seem to be very Conservative."
Goldsmith has threatened to field candidates in the general election, which must be held by next May, against every Conservative MP who does not show sympathy for his party's aims.

Opinion polls show such candidates would garner few votes, but with polls giving the opposition Labour Party a lead of at least 20 points, many Conservative MPs fear a Goldsmith candidate could win enough votes to make them lose their seats.
McAlpine told the BBC: "If the Referendum Party was standing, I think I would have to break a habit of a lifetime and probably vote for them."
He also said he would be prepared to chair the forthcoming Referendum Party conference at Brighton on October 19.
McAlpine said: "They have asked me to chair the conference and I will happily do that. I am interested in this conference because I think it's a conference that people of all parties can come to.
"It only has one aim...it aims to give people a referendum on Europe, to give them a choice."

McAlpine's defection could hardly have come at worse moment for Major. Apart from deep divisions over Europe, the Conservatives have in recent days been mired in a persistent row over parliamentary corruption.
Major on Sunday issued an angry rebuttal of claims that an aide tried to cover up accusations against a former minister.

Long-running allegations that former trade minister Neil Hamilton improperly took cash in return for asking parliamentary questions took a new twist on Sunday when newspapers reported that one of Major's aides had tried to influence a parliamentary investigation into the affair in 1994.
